definition: Solving a task with no examples at all — only an instruction — relying on knowledge already in the model.
details: Zero-shot means the model never saw a labeled example of the task, yet answers from its instruction and pre-trained knowledge. LLMs can reason zero-shot by being asked to think step by step, a simple technique that matches or beats earlier few-shot methods on many benchmarks.

explainer.lead: Zero-shot learning solves a task with no examples at all, using only an instruction and the knowledge already in the model. It matters because it lets models handle tasks they were never shown examples of.

tiers.eli5: You ask the model to do something it has never been shown how to do, and it works it out from what it already knows.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on it when labeled examples are unavailable, often pairing it with step-by-step reasoning. A pitfall is that performance is less predictable than with examples, especially on niche or unusual tasks.
tiers.paperLevel: The model receives no labeled example of the task and answers from its instruction and pre-trained knowledge; prompting step-by-step reasoning zero-shot can match or beat earlier few-shot methods on many benchmarks, with task-dependent limits.

explainer.example: Given only the instruction to classify a review as positive or negative, a model labels it correctly without any labeled training examples.

citation.title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
citation.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS)
